newsitem.title: USA: Bank proposal has inadequate protection -- US SEC.
newsitem.headline: Bank proposal has inadequate protection -- US SEC.

text.p: One of the leading Congressional proposals to modernize U.S. bank laws fails to adequately protect securities investors and includes too many loopholes for financial institutions, the nation's top securities regulator said Thursday.

Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt said the proposal, H.R. 268 introduced by Rep Marge Roukema, "would not provide adequate investor protection to the large number of customers buying securities through or obtaining investment advice from banks."

In prepared testimony for a House banking subcommittee chaired by Roukema, a New Jersey Republican, Levitt argued that investors who bought securities from banks would receive "a different, and in our view a lower, standard of protection than do investors who buy securities from broker-dealers."

Levitt added that other provisions of the bill were also "unacceptable" to the SEC, including mutual fund regulations for banks, arbitration provisions, and an "open-ended exemption" for banks dealing in "qualified financial contracts," which could potentially include any securities contract.
The Roukema bill does "make a useful contribution to the ongoing debate," Levitt said.

On the controversial issue of allowing financial and commercial companies to merge, Levitt said that, viewed from the securities perspective, "the commission has no objections to allowing commercial entities to engage in the securities business."
Roukema's bill would allow financial companies to do up to 25 percent of their business in non-financial activities, but other proposals impose no limits on combined companies.
Several of the largest U.S. securities firms have been owned by or affiliated with major commercial enterprises, Levitt noted.
"These affiliations have not impaired the commission's ability to oversee registered broker-dealers and do not appear to have resulted in the potential abuses targeted by banking regulation."
